rules.text: Use generous negative space. Readability comes before density — a page that looks busy gets skimmed, not read.

Write for a reader at the team's own technical level: keep most explanations brief, and never talk down or over-explain. Push real depth into sub-pages or expandable/collapsible panels instead of lengthening the main text.
Never use a term before it is defined. Define it on first use, or link to where it is defined, before relying on it elsewhere.
Use large, easy-to-read fonts everywhere. No rendered text may fall below the house-style minimum size.
Illustrate processes and concepts with real SVG diagrams — never ASCII art, and never a screenshot standing in for a diagram.
Use a table for any apples-to-apples comparison instead of describing it in prose.
Split content into new sections or sub-pages rather than cramming it all onto one page. A reader who bores easily should never face one long scroll.
Keep paragraphs short. A reader disengages from long text runs; break up anything past the house-style word limit for a paragraph.
Cite every factual claim back to its original source — a file path, a document, or another durable reference — so a reader can verify it independently.
Put caveats, notes, and asides in a callout component, never inline as a parenthetical or a footnote-like aside in body prose.
Use bold text to highlight the handful of most important topics on a page — not as routine emphasis sprinkled throughout.
Prefer a single sentence per bullet. A bullet that needs two or more sentences is usually better as its own short paragraph or broken into separate bullets.
Reach for a diagram, table, callout, or bullet list first. Write a prose paragraph only when none of those fit the content, and keep it short even then.
Leave generous vertical space between sections. Never shrink text to make it fit — route an aside into a callout or an on-demand panel instead of cramming it in at a smaller size.
A defined term shows its definition in a popover or a slide-out/slide-up panel on hover or click. Never use a modal dialog for this — modals behave badly on mobile.
Hide deep detail behind an interaction — an accordion, or a clickable diagram region that opens a side or bottom panel — instead of showing it by default.
A callout's background spans the full column width even when its text is narrower than the column.
Prefer a list or table with inline code over prose cluttered with inline code. Inline code must stay legible — never use a striped or alternating background behind it.

Tag every code or data example as Real (generated fresh from the code — for example an actual JSON payload mapped to its schema) or Illustrative (hand-written to explain a concept). Never leave an example untagged, and prefer a real, end-to-end scenario walkthrough (call, then result, then who handles it next and why) over an abstract description.
Prefer an "X mapped to Y" matrix over prose whenever the content describes a mapping between two sets (for example, callers mapped to the actions each one takes).
Never cite an internal ticket, task, or decision-record code as a reference — a reader outside the project cannot look it up. Cite a file path or a plain description instead.
A file-path reference links to the real file on its branch on GitHub, opening in a new tab.
Navigating to a page lands the reader at its top, not wherever a previous page happened to be scrolled to.
Diagram text must never overflow its box — wrap or resize it rather than letting it spill past its boundary.
Use a real table element for tabular data — never a div-based layout that merely looks like a table.
Keep diagram node text short and at a consistent font size. Put further detail on demand, in a click-to-open panel, rather than packing it into the node itself.
Let a diagram use the available horizontal space and degrade gracefully at narrow widths, rather than shrinking its text illegibly to fit.
Every bar chart ships a real data table next to it, so the same information reaches a reader who skims and a reader who needs the exact values.
Offer a "Start here" kickoff page suited to presenting the artifact live in a meeting, alongside its regular pages.
When proposing a change to an existing plan, frame it as "same direction, N refinements": show what stays the same, and justify each individual change in detail.
Illustrate an abstract concept with concrete toy code, kept to at most 50 lines per file.
Render code with syntax highlighting, unwrapped and horizontally scrollable, at a slightly smaller font than body text.
When showing what changed, use one large, color-coded diagram with a consistent legend for a three-way distinction such as identical, refactored, and new.
An optional live Q&A board is answered on demand — never by an always-on background loop.
Generate page numbering, navigation, and the pager from the artifact's own structure — never hand-number a page.
Define a term with a popover on its first mention per page, and keep the full glossary on the generated Terms page.
When there is more to say than a tight space allows — a table cell, a caption, a long parenthetical — put the extra detail in a panel and keep one plain sentence inline.
Make a diagram element clickable whenever there is real detail behind it — what it is, the files that implement it, the functions involved — and say so in the caption.
Give a flow, decision, or sequence step a clickable detail panel, and chain a multi-step sequence together so a reader can move to the next or previous step from inside it.
Annotate a field or value inside a data structure — a JSON payload, a table row, a code sample — with a clickable marker rather than a parenthetical.
Put a payload, a log, or a full example too large to show inline into a panel, and label it Real or Illustrative the same as any other example.
Never put the page's main claim, or anything a reader must know to follow along, only inside a panel — state it on the page itself, and use a panel only for supporting detail.
Never tell a reader to click, tap, or select something that isn't actually clickable — a caption that names an interaction only works when the element it describes is a real trigger.
Keep a panel's own content to one level — link out to a term or another page from inside it rather than chaining it into a second panel.

Every clickable trigger and every link that opens in a new tab carries a visible cue — an underline style and a small icon matched to what it does — so a reader can tell it's interactive, and what clicking it will do, before they click it.
